prompt: In the fake supplier invoice case, what made the requests believable?
options: The fraudster impersonated a real supplier that the companies already worked with
The emails were sent in the middle of the night
The invoices were extremely small
The emails contained viruses
explanation: The invoices looked routine because the supplier was real and the relationship was genuine. Borrowed trust was the whole trick.

prompt: What would most likely have stopped payment on the fake invoices?
options: Confirming bank details and unusual payments with the real supplier through a separate known channel
Using longer passwords
Installing a newer browser
Blocking every attachment
explanation: Nothing was hacked. A phone call to a number already on file would have exposed the fraud.

prompt: You receive a 'security alert' saying someone used your password, with a Change password button. What is the best action?
options: Click the button
Go to the service's website directly and check your security settings there
Reply and ask if it is real
Forward it to friends as a warning
explanation: This is the 2016 trick. If the alert is real, the same information is in your account settings when you go there yourself.

prompt: The 2016 alert used a shortened link. Why does that help an attacker?
options: It hides the destination, so the fake page is not obvious
It makes the page load faster
It encrypts the password
It switches off email filters
explanation: A shortened link hides where it goes, so the victim cannot spot a suspicious address before clicking.

prompt: Someone phones saying they are from internal IT and asks you to sign in to a page they are texting you. What do you do?
options: Follow along, because they sound professional
End the call and contact IT through a number from the company directory
Ask for their name and then continue
Sign in, but do not read out your password
explanation: This is the 2020 social media case. Never trust a caller who contacted you. Call back on a number you already know.

prompt: What do all three cases have in common?
options: The attackers exploited trust in a familiar person, brand or role, and relied on someone acting without checking
They all required advanced hacking of firewalls
They all started with a lost laptop
They only affected small companies
explanation: Different channels, same method: a trusted identity and a person who acts before checking.

prompt: Which type of sign-in is hardest to phish, because it only works on the real website?
options: Security keys or passkeys
Four-digit PINs
Security questions
Passwords with symbols
explanation: Security keys and passkeys are tied to the genuine website, so they refuse to work on a fake page, even if a person is fooled.

prompt: A finance clerk gets an email from a known supplier: 'New bank account details, effective immediately. The next invoice is due Friday.' What should the clerk do?
options: Update the details and pay
Phone the supplier on a number already on file before changing anything
Reply asking if the new details are correct
Update the details but pay only half
explanation: A changed bank account is the classic invoice fraud. Replying reaches the fraudster, so verify by phone using a known number.
